title: Git Lab: version control, taught
summary: Six lessons in Git snapshots, branches, merge, rebase, reset and recovery; 29 keyboard-based tasks. Virtual-lab reading resources; no player acceptance claimed.
prerequisites: Know what a file and a folder are, and that a file's contents can change.
Can enter shell commands: create a file with echo text > file, read it with cat, and list files with ls. Understand that rm deletes a file.

lessons.title: Snapshots: working tree, staging area, commit
Merge: bringing lines of work together
Rebase: replaying work on a new base
Reset: moving the branch, the staging area and the files

activities.prompt:
The harbor log has two files and no repository. Make one commit named exactly “Start the harbor log” that holds both files, and leave nothing unstaged or untracked.

Input requirement: keyboard command entry in a virtual Git player. In a text-only reader, write the command plan and explanation with a keyboard and self-check against the stated goals; this does not execute commands or grade the task. A remote alone is insufficient.

Starting commands:
echo 06:00 tide high > tides.txt
echo Berth 4 free > berths.txt
activities.explanation:
Self-check your proposed final state:
- History, newest first: Start the harbor log.
- No staged changes, unstaged changes or untracked files remain.
Explain why your commands reach these goals. Worked answers, when supplied, are in the lesson reading’s final hint.

activities.prompt:

Starting commands:

echo Berth 4 free > berths.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Start the harbor log"
echo Berth 5 free > berths.txt
echo 06:00 tide high, check > tides.txt
activities.explanation:
Self-check your proposed final state:
- History, newest first: Fix berth number → Start the harbor log.
- The current commit is named “Fix berth number”.
- Last committed version of berths.txt: 'Berth 5 free' (ending with a newline).
- Last committed version of tides.txt: '06:00 tide high' (ending with a newline).
- Working file tides.txt: '06:00 tide high, check' (ending with a newline).
- Staged version of tides.txt: '06:00 tide high' (ending with a newline).
Explain why your commands reach these goals. Worked answers, when supplied, are in the lesson reading’s final hint.
